claims.title: soldPrice parsed with parseFloat before validating it's a clean numeric string
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**soldPrice parsed with parseFloat before validating it's a clean numeric string**

`parseFloat(it.soldPrice)` will silently succeed on partially-numeric strings like "25 USD" or "$25" would fail (parseFloat("$25") -> NaN, correctly filtered), but a value like "25.99 (Buy It Now)" would parse to 25.99 without any indication the field format changed. If the upstream API changes soldPrice formatting, this could silently produce plausible-looking but wrong prices rather than failing loudly. Low risk given the API is third-party and undocumented in the diff, but worth a comment noting the expected format assumption.

claims.title: SoldComps API failures and empty-results are logged identically to the removed dead-source failures, with no distinction for auth errors
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**SoldComps API failures and empty-results are logged identically to the removed dead-source failures, with no distinction for auth errors**

`searchEbaySoldComps` returns `[]` on missing API key, HTTP error, and any thrown exception, all via `console.warn`. Given this PR is explicitly a fix for the fact that a prior silent comp-source failure went undetected for ~2 weeks (per the PR description), a 401 (bad/expired SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY) will look identical in logs/behavior to a legitimate 'zero sold comps for this query' or a transient timeout. Since this is the exact failure mode the PR is fixing (dead source silently returning empty), consider logging the HTTP status explicitly and/or incrementing a metric so a future silent-key-rotation-failure doesn't reproduce the same multi-week blind spot this PR is remediating.

claims.title: No rate limiting / retry handling for free-tier 100 searches/month cap
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**No rate limiting / retry handling for free-tier 100 searches/month cap**

The free SoldComps tier is capped at 100 searches/month per the PR description. There's no caching, dedup across concurrent calls, or quota-exhaustion detection (e.g. distinguishing a 429/quota error from a generic failure) — a 429 will just log a warning and silently return `[]`, degrading indistinguishably from "no comps found", making it hard to detect quota exhaustion in production. Consider logging a distinct warning for 429/402 status codes so operators can tell quota exhaustion apart from a transient failure.

claims.title: condition hardcoded to 'Not specified' discarding SoldComps item quality
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**condition hardcoded to 'Not specified' discarding SoldComps item quality**

`EbayAdapter.searchSoldComps` maps every `PlatformComp.condition` to the literal `'Not specified'` regardless of what `SoldListing` might convey, since `SoldListing` doesn't carry a condition field. This is consistent with `ebay-soldcomps.ts` not returning condition, but worth flagging: `PlatformComp` callers relying on condition for filtering/adjustment will silently treat all eBay sold comps as unknown condition even if better signal is available from the API's item payload (`SoldCompsItem` doesn't currently capture condition either).

claims.title: Comment above searchEbayActiveWithFallback slightly overstates guarantee
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Comment above searchEbayActiveWithFallback slightly overstates guarantee**

The comment states "a healthy Browse API never costs a SerpAPI request," which is accurate given the logic (browseResults.length > 0 short-circuits). However it doesn't mention that a Browse API call which throws (rather than returning an empty array) will propagate and skip the fallback entirely — Promise.all in the caller will reject the whole batch. If searchEbayActive can throw on transient errors, this fallback provides no resilience in that case, which the comment doesn't caveat.

claims.title: SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY read directly from process.env instead of via ApiKeys/apiKeys plumbing
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY read directly from process.env instead of via ApiKeys/apiKeys plumbing**

Every other external API key in this pipeline (serpapi, poshmarkCookies, anthropic, etc.) is threaded through the `ApiKeys` object passed into `runStep3PricingResearch` and its helpers, but `searchEbaySoldComps` reads `process.env.SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY` directly. This breaks the existing pattern of per-request/user-scoped key injection used elsewhere in this file (e.g. `apiKeys.serpapi`, `apiKeys.poshmarkCookies`), makes the function harder to test/mock, and means this call site silently depends on a different configuration mechanism than its neighbors in the same `Promise.all`. If `ApiKeys` is meant to represent user-supplied/overridable keys, this diverges from that model without explanation.

claims.title: condition hardcoded to 'Not specified' loses data already available from SoldComps API response
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**condition hardcoded to 'Not specified' loses data already available from SoldComps API response**

`EbayAdapter.searchSoldComps` now maps SoldComps results to `PlatformComp` with `condition: 'Not specified'` unconditionally. Since `SoldListing` (from `ebay-soldcomps.ts`) doesn't carry a condition field at all, this is consistent with the current type, but it means condition data is being discarded/never fetched from the SoldComps API even though the API may expose it (mirroring `SoldCompsItem`'s title/soldPrice/endedAt/url fields already parsed). This silently degrades comp quality data for the eBay adapter path without any indication this is a stub.

claims.title: parseFloat on soldPrice has no currency/locale safeguard
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**parseFloat on soldPrice has no currency/locale safeguard**

`parseFloat(it.soldPrice)` will silently misparse or NaN-out on any currency-prefixed value (e.g. "$123.45", "US $123.45", or a value with thousands separators like "1,234.56"). Since the result is filtered by `priceCents > 0`, a currency-prefixed price string returns `NaN`, is caught by `Number.isFinite(price) ? ... : 0`, and the whole row is silently dropped by the final filter -- with no log line indicating a parse failure occurred, only a quietly smaller result set. Given this client exists specifically to fix a previously-undetected silent comp collapse, a parse failure here would reproduce the same class of bug without any signal.

claims.title: searchSoldComps limit parameter from PlatformSDK not honored
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**searchSoldComps limit parameter from PlatformSDK not honored**

If `PlatformSDK.searchSoldComps` accepts an optional limit/options argument (as referenced by the prior review comment and the MCP dispatcher passing `input.limit`), this implementation ignores it entirely and returns every row SoldComps returns unbounded. This is a correctness gap for any caller requesting a bounded result set, not just a nice-to-have.

claims.title: SoldComps price parsing can silently drop all comps on currency-formatted strings
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**SoldComps price parsing can silently drop all comps on currency-formatted strings**

`parseFloat(it.soldPrice)` on a price string like `"$123.45"` or `"1,234.56"` returns `NaN` for a leading `$`, or truncates at the comma for thousands-separated values (`parseFloat("1,234.56")` === `1`). Since the response schema for `soldPrice` is unverified and the code has no stripping of currency symbols/separators, this can cause `priceCents` to be `0` or wildly wrong for every row, silently filtered out by the `priceCents > 0` check (rows would vanish) or, worse, pass through with a wrong price (e.g. `"1,234.56"` -> `100` cents instead of `123456` cents).

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
        const price = it.soldPrice ? parseFloat(it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')) : NaN
```

claims.title: SerpAPI active-listing fallback price filter/mapping may reference a nonexistent field
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**SerpAPI active-listing fallback price filter/mapping may reference a nonexistent field**

The new `fetchEbayActiveSerpApi` reads `price.extracted` instead of the previously used `price.extracted_value` (still used elsewhere in this same file for `SerpShoppingResult`). If SerpAPI's eBay plain-search engine actually returns `extracted_value` (consistent with its other engines), this filter (`r.price?.extracted`) will always be falsy, silently dropping every result and making the fallback permanently dead code returning `[]`.

claims.title: soldPrice/priceCents comment overstates currency-symbol robustness
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**soldPrice/priceCents comment overstates currency-symbol robustness**

The comment claims stripping `[^0-9.-]` handles a future `"$1,234.56"` format "correctly," but this regex strips commas along with the currency symbol, turning `"$1,234.56"` into `"1234.56"` — that part is actually fine. However, the same strip also collapses a legitimately negative or malformed string in unexpected ways (e.g. a stray `-` anywhere in the string survives the filter and can produce a wrong sign via `parseFloat`). More importantly, the comment's framing implies this parsing is robust against arbitrary currency formats, which isn't fully true for formats using a different decimal separator (e.g. European `"1.234,56"` would parse as `1.234` cents-scaled incorrectly). Consider narrowing the comment to state it only handles USD-style `$`/comma formatting, or add a stricter format guard.

A future maintainer could reasonably assume the 503 risk still applies to this exact code today, when in fact it was empirically the Sold filter, not plain search, that eBay blocked (per the PR description, plain search returns 200 OK in ~2.3s). Consider clarifying that the 503 evidence is historical context for the *replaced* Sold-filter fetcher, not a current risk of this plain-search function.

claims.title: SoldComps price parsed with a lossy currency-stripping regex that also strips thousands-separator commas incorrectly
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**SoldComps price parsed with a lossy currency-stripping regex that also strips thousands-separator commas incorrectly**

`it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')` strips currency symbols and commas together. For a price like "$1,234.56" this produces "1234.56" (correct, by coincidence, since comma is simply dropped), but for a European-style price such as "1.234,56" it would produce "1.234.56" -> `parseFloat` returns `1.234`, silently truncating the value by three orders of magnitude with no error or warning. Given the comment above acknowledges a future format change is anticipated ("a future format change (e.g. '$1,234.56')"), the current regex doesn't actually handle thousands separators correctly — it only works for USD-style formatting by accident, and a malformed/foreign-format price will silently produce a wrong (not obviously invalid) `priceCents` value that passes the `priceCents > 0` filter and gets inserted as real pricing evidence.

`it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')` strips currency symbols but not comma thousands separators, since commas are simply removed rather than treated as a separator. claims.title: Fragile currency parsing could silently zero out non-numeric or unexpected soldPrice formats
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Fragile currency parsing could silently zero out non-numeric or unexpected soldPrice formats**

`it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')` strips everything except digits, `.` and `-`. A thousands-separator format like "1,234.56" becomes "1234.56" correctly, but any format with multiple `.`/`-` characters (e.g. a stray dash in a price range or a malformed string) would produce a value that `parseFloat` parses partially/incorrectly rather than failing, and the resulting NaN-guard (`Number.isFinite(price) ? ... : 0`) only catches a fully-non-numeric string, not a partially-valid one — the row would still be inserted with a silently wrong price rather than being dropped. Since this is the primary sold-price source being restored, consider validating the parsed price against a stricter pattern before accepting it.

claims.title: CompProvider union doesn't include the 'ebay_browse'/'serpapi' provider tags used for active-listing rows in a type-consistent way
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**CompProvider union doesn't include the 'ebay_browse'/'serpapi' provider tags used for active-listing rows in a type-consistent way**

`CompProvider` is defined as `'soldcomps' | 'ebay_browse' | 'serpapi' | 'poshmark_direct' | 'reddit_claude'` and `PricingComp.provider` is typed `CompProvider | null`, but in step3-pricing-research.ts the in-flight `compRows`/`activeRows` arrays that build these objects are typed with `provider: string | null` (see the local interface literal added around the compRows push), not `CompProvider | null`. This means a typo or new provider string added later in step3 (e.g. `provider: 'ebay_broswe'`) would not be caught by the type checker even though a proper union type exists for exactly this purpose.

claims.title: searchSoldComps ignores per-user SoldComps key and reads process.env directly
claims.text:
🔴 **High**

**searchSoldComps ignores per-user SoldComps key and reads process.env directly**

This reads `process.env.SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY` directly rather than accepting an injected/per-user key. Elsewhere in this PR (`step3-pricing-research.ts`, `user-api-keys.ts`), the SoldComps key is threaded per-user via `apiKeys.soldcomps`. Any caller of this adapter method (e.g. via `mcp-server.ts`, which resolves per-user credentials) will bypass that user's configured key and fall back to whatever key happens to be set in the server process env, which may belong to a different user or be unset entirely for a user who has their own key configured. Also note `_query` was previously unused-prefixed but is now used without a corresponding `limit`/options parameter, even though `PlatformSDK.searchSoldComps` (per the MCP dispatcher usage referenced in the review body) is expected to accept an optional `limit`.

claims.text:

**searchSoldComps drops the optional limit parameter from PlatformSDK**

The `SoldListing[]` results from `searchEbaySoldComps` are mapped and returned unbounded. If `PlatformSDK.searchSoldComps` is expected to accept an optional `limit` (as used by the MCP dispatcher passing `input.limit`), this signature drops it entirely, so callers requesting a small result set still get every row SoldComps returns.

claims.title: Currency parsing regex will mis-parse negative-looking or multi-hyphen strings
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Currency parsing regex will mis-parse negative-looking or multi-hyphen strings**

`it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')` keeps both `.` and `-` characters. If the API ever returns something like a price range or a value containing a stray hyphen (e.g. `"$29.99-"` from a trailing dash, or multiple `.` from thousands-as-period formats in other locales), `parseFloat` will parse only the leading numeric run and silently ignore the rest rather than failing loudly — the `Number.isFinite` check won't catch a partially-correct parse. This is low-risk given the currently-observed format is a bare number, but worth tightening (e.g. strip everything but digits and a single decimal point, or reject strings containing `-` entirely) since the whole point of this fallback path per the comment is to guard against a future format change.

claims.title: Currency parsing strips digits from thousands separators inconsistently
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Currency parsing strips digits from thousands separators inconsistently**

`it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, '')` strips a leading `$` but also silently strips a comma thousands separator without removing the digits around it (e.g. "$1,234.56" becomes "1234.56", which happens to be correct here) — but this only works because `,` is stripped entirely rather than treated as a separator; if SoldComps ever formats with a `.` as a thousands separator and `,` as decimal (some locales), this would silently produce a wrong value (e.g. "1.234,56" -> "1.234.56" -> `parseFloat` truncates at the second `.`, yielding 1.234). This is speculative on future format changes but worth a narrower regex or explicit locale assumption in the comment.

claims.title: fetchEbayActiveSerpApi filters on price.extracted; verify this matches SerpAPI's actual eBay engine response field
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**fetchEbayActiveSerpApi filters on price.extracted; verify this matches SerpAPI's actual eBay engine response field**

The new fallback filters/maps on `r.price?.extracted` (`SerpApiEbayActiveResult.price?: { extracted?: number }`), diverging from the file's other SerpAPI response type (`SerpShoppingResult`) which uses `extracted_price` at the top level per a comment noting the shopping engine's real field name was discovered via live testing. If the eBay engine's plain-search response nests the numeric price under a different key than `extracted`, every row is filtered out here and the fallback silently becomes dead code returning `[]` — which is exactly the class of bug this PR is fixing for the shopping engine. The PR body claims this was live-tested ("52 real active listings"), so this may already be correct, but given the sibling field-name bug just fixed in this same file, this is worth an explicit test fixture asserting the exact response shape rather than relying on a one-off manual test.

claims.title: retailResult now always relies on scoreCompRelevance / apiKeys.anthropic, changing prior no-key behavior
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**retailResult now always relies on scoreCompRelevance / apiKeys.anthropic, changing prior no-key behavior**

Previously `fetchRetailPrice` returned a retail price purely from the cheapest `new`-condition Google Shopping result, independent of any Anthropic key. Now `retailRelevance` is only computed `if (apiKeys.anthropic && retailCandidates.length > 0)`, otherwise it's an empty `Map`, which means `relevantRetail` filters out every candidate (since `relevance_score !== null` will never be true) whenever `apiKeys.anthropic` is unset — so retail pricing silently disappears entirely for any user without an Anthropic key configured, not just degrading match quality. This is an intentional relevance-gating design per the surrounding comment, but it's worth confirming this fail-closed behavior (no retail price shown at all without an Anthropic key) is the desired tradeoff versus the previous unconditional-but-less-accurate retail price.

claims.title: fetchEbayActiveSerpApi rows are missing a soldAt/provider consistency guard versus ActiveListing type
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**fetchEbayActiveSerpApi rows are missing a soldAt/provider consistency guard versus ActiveListing type**

The mapped objects here satisfy the `ActiveListing` interface (`title`, `priceCents`, `url`, `condition`, `provider`), but the filter above only checks `r.title && r.price?.extracted && r.link` — there is no numeric-validity guard equivalent to the old code's `priceCents > 0` post-filter. If `r.price.extracted` is a truthy but non-numeric-like value (unlikely given the type, but the raw JSON is untyped `unknown` cast through the interface), `Math.round(NaN)` would produce `NaN` for `priceCents`, which would then pass through as a comp row with an invalid price. Consider adding `Number.isFinite(priceCents)` back as a safety net.

claims.title: Malformed soldPrice silently coerces to 0 instead of being dropped
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Malformed soldPrice silently coerces to 0 instead of being dropped**

When `it.soldPrice` fails to parse as a finite number (e.g. an unexpected format), `Number.isFinite(price) ? Math.round(price * 100) : 0` produces `priceCents: 0` rather than treating the row as invalid. The downstream filter `it.priceCents > 0` does drop these `0`-priced rows before they reach callers, so this doesn't currently insert bad $0 comps — but the coercion-to-0-then-filter pattern silently discards a parse failure without any log line, unlike the analogous `soldAt` parse-failure path just above it which is also silently dropped without a warning. A `console.warn` when `price` parsing fails would let operators distinguish "provider returned malformed price" from "provider returned no comps" when comp counts drop unexpectedly — the exact class of problem this PR exists to fix.

claims.title: CompProvider union type doesn't cover all provider values actually written to pricing_comps.provider
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**CompProvider union type doesn't cover all provider values actually written to pricing_comps.provider**

The `CompProvider` union is `'soldcomps' | 'ebay_browse' | 'serpapi' | 'poshmark_direct' | 'reddit_claude' | 'manual'`, but the DB column added in `0023_pricing_comps_provider.sql` is a plain `text` with no CHECK constraint, and application code writes provider values that must stay in sync manually (e.g. `provider: item.provider` from `ActiveListing.provider` which is typed `'ebay_browse' | 'serpapi'`, matching fine here). This is low risk today since all current call sites in the diff use values within the union, but there's no compile-time or DB-time enforcement tying the TS union to what's actually persisted, so a future addition of a provider string in one file without updating this type would silently produce untyped/mismatched data with no error.

claims.text:

**Sync-platform call sites construct EbayAdapter without a per-user SoldComps key**

The constructor's default parameter `private readonly soldcompsApiKey: string = process.env.SOLDCOMPS_API_KEY ?? ''` means any call site that constructs `EbayAdapter` without explicitly passing a second argument (the comment mentions "sync-platform-* Inngest functions") will silently fall back to a global env var rather than a per-user key, even though `user-api-keys.ts` now models `soldcomps` as a per-user credential. This is a design inconsistency: `mcp-server.ts`'s `getAdapter` correctly threads the per-user key, but other constructors of `EbayAdapter` (not shown in this diff) may still get single-tenant behavior for a nominally per-user credential. If SoldComps searches from those other call sites are expected to use per-user keys like the rest of the per-user credential system, this silently uses the wrong key instead of failing loudly.

claims.title: Currency parsing silently coerces malformed soldPrice strings to 0 rather than dropping the row
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**Currency parsing silently coerces malformed soldPrice strings to 0 rather than dropping the row**

`parseFloat(it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, ''))` on a value like `"Best Offer"` or `"Free"` (with no digits at all) produces `NaN` via `parseFloat('')`, which correctly gets filtered by `Number.isFinite(price) ? ... : 0` and then dropped by `.filter(it => it.priceCents > 0 ...)`. However, a malformed value containing stray digits unrelated to price (e.g. a listing ID embedded in the string, or a range like `"$100-$150"` which strips to `"100-150"` and parses as `100`) would silently produce a wrong-but-plausible price rather than being rejected. This is a low-confidence edge case since the comment states the live-tested format is a bare numeric string, but the defensive stripping logic itself doesn't validate the stripped string matches a single well-formed number before parsing.

claims.title: Retail relevance/luxury filtering applies before `removeOutlierComps`, but outlier removal on `RetailCandidate[]` needs a `sale_price_cents`-shaped input
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**Retail relevance/luxury filtering applies before `removeOutlierComps`, but outlier removal on `RetailCandidate[]` needs a `sale_price_cents`-shaped input**

`relevantRetail` builds objects with `priceCents` as the raw field name (from `RetailCandidate`), then adds `adjusted_price_cents`. `removeOutlierComps` is used elsewhere in this file against arrays whose price field is `sale_price_cents` (see `compRows`/`activeRows` usage). If `removeOutlierComps` reads `sale_price_cents` internally, `filteredRetail` here would silently no-op (or worse, misbehave) because `relevantRetail` objects only carry `priceCents`/`adjusted_price_cents`, not `sale_price_cents`. This isn't confirmed from the diff since `removeOutlierComps`'s implementation isn't shown, so treat this as a question rather than a confirmed bug — but it's worth an explicit check given the field name mismatch is visible in the diff.

claims.title: SoldComps price parsing on 'soldPrice' field could produce priceCents=0 for legitimately free/very-cheap items and silently drop them
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**SoldComps price parsing on 'soldPrice' field could produce priceCents=0 for legitimately free/very-cheap items and silently drop them**

`parseFloat(it.soldPrice.replace(/[^0-9.-]/g, ''))` followed by `.filter((it) => it.priceCents > 0 ...)` means any comp that legitimately sold for $0.00 (unlikely but possible for bundled/promotional listings) or whose price string fails to parse (`NaN` -> `Number.isFinite` false -> `priceCents = 0`) is silently dropped with no distinguishing log between 'parse failed' and 'genuinely zero price'. This matches the pattern used elsewhere in the file (e.g., the old sold-comps fetcher), so it's a low-impact consistency nit rather than a new regression.

claims.title: listingUrl accepted without scheme validation, enabling stored javascript: URI in a rendered <a href>
claims.text:
🟡 **Medium**

**listingUrl accepted without scheme validation, enabling stored javascript: URI in a rendered <a href>**

`body.listingUrl` is stored verbatim (only trimmed) with no scheme allow-list check. `EvidenceDrawer.tsx` renders `comp.listing_url` directly as an `<a href={...}>` for every comp including manual ones, without the `isUrl()` guard used elsewhere in that same component. A caller could submit `listingUrl: 'javascript:alert(document.cookie)'`, which would be stored and rendered as a clickable link. Since `pricing_comps` has no owner-scoped RLS per this route's own comment, any authenticated user could write this to any listing_id they can guess, creating a stored XSS vector triggered when that listing's evidence drawer is viewed and the link clicked. Validate the URL has an `http(s)` scheme before persisting (or apply the same check client-side that `isUrl()` already implements, but do it server-side since this is the actual trust boundary).

*Suggested fix:*

```suggestion
    listing_url: body.listingUrl?.trim() && /^https?:\/\//i.test(body.listingUrl.trim()) ? body.listingUrl.trim() : null,
```

claims.title: pricing_comps DELETE route has no rate limiting or input length validation on compId
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**pricing_comps DELETE route has no rate limiting or input length validation on compId**

`body.compId` is used directly in a `.eq('id', body.compId)` filter without validating it's actually a UUID. If `compId` is not a valid UUID, Supabase/Postgres will likely just error the query (caught by the existing `deleteError` handling), so this is low risk, but adding a basic UUID shape check before the query would give a cleaner 400 instead of a 500 on malformed input.

claims.title: final_price_cents validation only rejects non-positive values, not NaN from unparsed strings
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**final_price_cents validation only rejects non-positive values, not NaN from unparsed strings**

The check `typeof body.finalPriceCents !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(...) || body.finalPriceCents <= 0` correctly guards against non-numeric/NaN/non-positive values, but there's no upper bound or integer check — a caller could send `0.5` cents or an extremely large float, which then gets silently `Math.round()`-ed. This is a minor validation gap, not a security issue given this is an authenticated same-user write, but worth tightening for defense in depth.

claims.title: EvidenceDrawer add-comp form pointer default for isActive comps sets sold_at path but skips soldAt validation
claims.text:
🟢 **Low**

**EvidenceDrawer add-comp form pointer default for isActive comps sets sold_at path but skips soldAt validation**

`submitManualComp` sends `isActive: addActive` but never collects/sends a `soldAt` date from the UI for non-active (sold) manual comps — the API route defaults `sold_at` to `body.soldAt ?? null` when not active, meaning every manually-added 'sold' comp will have `sold_at: null` despite being marked as sold rather than active. This is a UX/data-completeness gap: a sold comp with no sold date is indistinguishable from a data-entry error later, and downstream code that filters/sorts by `sold_at` may silently drop or misclassify these rows.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined — 429/402 (quota exhaustion, the free-tier-relevant case) already logs distinctly from other HTTP errors. Further splitting out 401/403/5xx is marginal value for a fail-soft fetcher that returns `[]` either way by design (matches every other comp source in this pipeline).

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined for this PR — explicitly deferred in the original plan: no caching/dedup/rate-limiting against the 100/month free cap, with the $9/mo Starter tier (2,000/mo) as the immediate next step if that proves too limiting. Not building speculative quota management before there's real usage data on how tight it actually is.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined as a group — SoldComps is a real, live-tested, US-only API (bare numeric strings like "380"/"29.99", ISO date-only endedAt); the comma/negative-hyphen/locale-format concerns are hypothetical for a format that's never been observed. The existing `Number.isFinite(price)` and `!isNaN(parsedDate.getTime())` guards already fail safely (drop the row via the `priceCents > 0`/`soldAt !== null` filter) rather than insert corrupted data if the format ever does change. Not adding speculative parsing for a format this API doesn't produce.

It's the correct field name for this specific engine, distinct from the Shopping engine's top-level `extracted_price`.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined — this is an intentional design change, not a regression. The prior "always trust the cheapest new-condition result" behavior is exactly what produced a fabricated retail price (a wrong-item $81 match, live-confirmed on a real listing this session). Fail-closed (no key/no score = no retail price shown) matches the existing `lowestActive` pattern for the same reason: a wrong price claim shown as fact is worse than showing none.

replies.body: Declined — intentional, and documented in the constructor comment: sync-platform-* call sites have no userId in scope, so the env-var default is the correct fallback there. mcp-server.ts (the userId-aware call site) passes the real per-user key.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined — same rationale as the other currency-parsing findings: this is real sold-comp data from a live API (numeric prices only), not free-text like "Best Offer"/"Free". The existing Number.isFinite guard already drops anything that doesn't parse rather than inserting bad data.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Confirmed non-issue — appreciate the explicit "treat as a question" framing. removeOutlierComps's actual signature is `<T extends { adjusted_price_cents: number }>`, it only ever reads adjusted_price_cents, never sale_price_cents. relevantRetail's objects carry adjusted_price_cents (added via the .map above), so this works correctly.

replies.author: joeblackwaslike
replies.body: Declined — same currency/edge-case rationale as the sibling findings on this file. A genuinely free/$0 sold comp is vanishingly unlikely for real eBay sold data and not worth the added complexity to special-case.
